overview: Stellantis is a Netherlands-incorporated global automaker formed in January 2021 from the merger of Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA) and PSA Group (Peugeot). It designs, manufactures, distributes and sells vehicles under 14 brands -- Jeep, Ram, Chrysler, Dodge, Peugeot, Citroen, Opel/Vauxhall, FIAT, Alfa Romeo, Maserati, DS, Lancia, Abarth and Leapmotor (distributed, not owned) -- through six reportable segments: North America, Enlarged Europe, Middle East & Africa, South America, China and India & Asia Pacific, and Maserati. It multi-lists on Euronext Paris (STLAP), Euronext Milan (STLAM) and the NYSE (STLA), and also runs captive financial-services joint ventures, a parts/service business and mobility brands (Free2move, Share Now).

business_model.summary: Primarily a capital-intensive hardware business: vehicle sales to dealers, distributors and fleets (shipment-based revenue recognition) drive the vast majority of revenue, supplemented by higher-margin parts/service/accessories and by dealer and retail financing income earned through captive finance subsidiaries and joint ventures (e.g., Stellantis Financial Services U.S., Banco Stellantis in Brazil, Chinese captive finance units). Revenue is transactional/cyclical rather than recurring -- tied to vehicle shipment volumes, pricing/incentives and mix (trucks/SUVs are far more profitable than small cars or BEVs).
business_model.customer_type: B2C retail via dealer networks, plus B2B fleet/government/commercial channels; financial services arm serves both dealers (floorplan financing) and retail customers (loans/leases)
business_model.geographic_mix: FY2025 net revenues of EUR153.5bn; shipments by segment: North America ~1.47m units, Enlarged Europe ~2.49m units, South America ~1.0m units, Middle East & Africa ~0.45m units, China/India/Asia Pacific ~0.06m units, Maserati ~8k units. North America and Europe together account for the large majority of profit despite roughly similar unit volumes, reflecting much higher vehicle value/mix in North America.

main_competitors: Chinese entrants (BYD, Leapmotor, other EV makers)
competitive_position.market_position: Mid-pack global volume manufacturer: #2 in the EU30 market with ~16% share (down from 18.3% in 2023), and #6 in the U.S. with ~7.6% share (down from 9.6% in 2023, behind GM, Toyota, Ford, Hyundai/Kia and Honda). Leader in EU30 light commercial vehicles (Pro One, ~28.6% share) and in the EU B-segment BEV niche (>31% share). Maserati is a small, declining luxury niche player.

moat_factors.description: Multi-brand architecture intended to spread platform, powertrain and software investment (STLA Large/Medium/Small/Frame, and the next-generation STLA One global platform) across 14 brands and ~5.5m annual shipments, though realized synergies have lagged plan

Spans mass-market to luxury and strong regional leadership positions (#1 in France, Italy, Portugal; leading European light-commercial-vehicle brand via Pro One), giving exposure across price points and vehicle types
In-house/JV financing (SFS U.S. ~40% share of Stellantis retail/lease financing) supports vehicle sales and dealer floorplan but also adds balance-sheet leverage and funding-market risk
Plants across NAFTA, Europe, South America and MEA provide some tariff/currency hedge flexibility, though U.S.-Mexico tariff exposure remains a material weakness

moat_factors.factor: Dealer network and local market leadership
moat_factors.description: Longstanding #1/#2 positions in core European markets (France, Italy, Spain) and strong U.S. truck/SUV brand equity (Jeep, Ram)

weaknesses: Losing U.S. and European market share for three consecutive years (U.S. 9.6% to 7.6% FY2023-FY2025; EU30 18.3% to 16.0%)
Quality and warranty issues associated with new platform/powertrain launches drove a large FY2025 change in warranty estimate
Negligible presence in China (~0.2% share) and broader Asia Pacific, ceding the world's largest EV/auto market largely to local and JV partners
Product portfolio gap and high dealer inventories in 2024-early 2025 forced pricing resets and incentive spending that hurt net pricing
Complex 14-brand structure increases execution and capital-allocation complexity versus more focused competitors

growth_drivers: FaSTLAne 2030 strategic plan (presented May 2026): targets net revenue growth from EUR154bn (2025) to EUR175bn by 2028 and EUR190bn by 2030, AOI margin of 5% by 2028 and 7% by 2030

More than 60 new vehicle models and ~50 significant refreshes planned through 2030 (29 BEV, 15 PHEV/REEV, 24 HEV, 39 ICE/MHEV), concentrated on four global brands (Jeep, Ram, Peugeot, FIAT) plus Pro One commercial vehicles (~70% of brand/product investment)

$13 billion U.S. manufacturing investment program (announced October 2025) over four years: Belvidere, Illinois plant reopening (Jeep Cherokee/Compass), new Ram midsize truck in Toledo, new large SUV in Warren, Michigan, next-gen Dodge Durango in Detroit, new engine plant in Kokomo, Indiana -- expected to raise U.S. production capacity ~50% and create 5,000+ jobs
Value Creation Program targeting ~EUR6 billion run-rate annual cost reductions by 2028 versus a 2025 baseline
Global platform consolidation: ~50% of global volumes on three global platforms (including new STLA One architecture) by 2030, reducing R&D/capex duplication

Manufacturing footprint optimization: >800,000 units of European capacity reduction targeted alongside utilization increases from ~60% to ~80% by 2030; North America utilization also targeted to reach ~80%

New partnerships to extend reach at lower capital cost: Leapmotor International (51% owned) for China-based EV distribution outside China; expanded Dongfeng Motor Group cooperation in China/Europe; Tata Motors cooperation in Asia Pacific/MEA/South America; exploratory talks with Jaguar Land Rover
Return of higher-margin ICE/HEMI powertrains (5.7L HEMI V-8 Ram 1500) responding to consumer demand softening for BEVs, improving near-term mix and profitability
Software-defined vehicle technology stack (STLA Brain, STLA SmartCockpit, STLA AutoDrive) launching from 2027, targeted on ~35% of volumes by 2030 and >70% by 2035

business.risk: Market share erosion in core NAFTA and Europe markets
business.description: U.S. share fell from 9.6% (2023) to 7.6% (2025); EU30 share fell from 18.3% to 16.0% over the same period, against resurgent GM/Toyota/Ford and Chinese entrants in Europe
A FY2025 change in estimate for contractual warranties added ~EUR4.1bn of charges; new platform/powertrain quality issues contributed to 2024-H1 2025 commercial headwinds

business.risk: EV demand uncertainty and program cancellations
business.description: Cancelled Ram 1500 BEV and other EV programs, wrote off capitalized development spend, exited the NextStar and ACC battery joint ventures and discontinued the hydrogen fuel cell program -- all reflecting miscalibrated prior EV bets
~0.2%-0.3% China market share leaves Stellantis dependent on JV partners (DPCA, Leapmotor, Dongfeng) in the world's largest and most competitive EV market

business.risk: Execution risk under new strategic plan
business.description: FaSTLAne 2030 targets (EUR190bn revenue, 7% AOI margin by 2030) require successful multi-year platform consolidation, cost cuts and new-model launches without repeating 2024-2025 execution failures

financial.risk: Negative industrial free cash flow despite a net cash balance sheet
financial.description: Industrial free cash flow was negative EUR4.5bn in FY2025 and negative EUR0.9bn in H1 2026; industrial net financial position nonetheless improved from net cash of EUR6.7bn (Dec 2025) to net cash of ~EUR10bn (June 2026), as EUR4.9bn of new hybrid perpetual notes issued in Q1 2026 outpaced the cash burn
S&P cut Stellantis to BBB- (negative outlook) and Moody's cut to Baa3 in February 2026, raising borrowing costs just as the company issues more debt/hybrid capital
Board suspended the dividend policy in February 2026 following the FY2025 net loss; no annual dividend will be paid in 2026, removing an income-support factor for the stock
FY2025 unfavorable FX translation cut net revenues by ~EUR5.9bn, driven by a weaker U.S. Dollar, Turkish Lira, Canadian Dollar and Brazilian Real versus the Euro
Large North American losses raise the risk that deferred tax assets may need to be de-recognized if future taxable income does not materialize as projected

regulatory.description: Non-compliance with EU fleet CO2 targets (93.6 g/km passenger cars from 2025, tightening to a 100% reduction from 2021 levels by 2035) triggers penalties of EUR95 per gram over target per vehicle registered

regulatory.risk: U.S. regulatory rollback creates planning uncertainty
regulatory.description: The 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act eliminated CAFE fines and the EPA's February 2026 decision eliminated GHG standards for light/medium/heavy-duty vehicles, reversing the basis for some prior EV investment and credit assumptions (Stellantis still recognized CAFE-related impairments/onerous-contract charges in FY2025)
China's CAFC/NEV credit regime and upcoming China 7 emissions and battery-safety rules add compliance complexity in a market where Stellantis has minimal scale to absorb the cost
Ongoing emissions-related class actions and securities litigation in the Netherlands, UK, Portugal, Germany, Austria and Israel tied to legacy FCA/PSA diesel vehicles

macro.description: Net tariff headwind now estimated at EUR1.0-1.2bn for FY2026 (after a EUR0.4bn IEEPA refund); the new 2026 Jeep Cherokee, produced in Toluca, Mexico, is specifically flagged as exposed to significant tariff-driven profitability pressure

Vehicle demand is highly sensitive to consumer confidence, interest rates and financing availability/cost; central bank rate cuts in 2024-2025 provide some relief but credit costs remain a swing factor
FY2025/H1 2026 filings specifically flag the Iran conflict and broader global instability as sources of potential supply-chain disruption and energy/logistics cost inflation

macro.risk: Raw material and commodity cost volatility
macro.description: Exposure to steel, aluminum, battery materials (lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite) and precious metals (platinum, palladium, rhodium) pricing

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global auto industry is mature and intensely competitive, with slow-growing mature markets (US industry sales +1.6% in 2025, EU30 +0.9%) offset by faster growth in India/Asia Pacific (+4.5%) and continued share gains by Chinese EV manufacturers in both home and export markets. Regulatory divergence is widening: the EU is tightening CO2 targets toward 2035, while the US rolled back CAFE fines and GHG rules in 2025-2026, creating a bifurcated planning environment for global OEMs.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - vehicle sales are discretionary, financing-dependent and highly correlated with consumer confidence, interest rates and employment; Stellantis also runs structurally negative working capital, amplifying the cash-flow impact of any shipment downturn or plant shutdown
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high indirect sensitivity via consumer/dealer financing costs and demand, plus direct exposure through the financial-services JV funding base and the company's own debt refinancing (recent high-coupon hybrid perpetual notes issued at 6.25%-8.25%)
key_input_costs: Battery raw materials (lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, manganese)
Precious metals (platinum, palladium, rhodium) for catalytic converters

recent_developments.event: Reported FY2025 net loss of EUR22.3bn on EUR153.5bn revenue, driven by ~EUR25.4bn of adjustments excluded from AOI: platform impairments (EUR6.6bn, mostly North America), product plan realignment/program cancellation costs (EUR9.1bn), a warranty estimate change (EUR4.1bn), battery JV exits/NextStar and ACC write-downs (EUR2.1bn), and hydrogen fuel cell program discontinuation (EUR1.1bn)
Board suspended the dividend policy (no FY2025 dividend to be paid in 2026); S&P downgraded Stellantis to BBB- (negative outlook) and Moody's to Baa3
Agreed to sell its 49% stake in NextStar Energy (Canadian battery JV with LG Energy Solution) to LG, closing March 2026, completing the planned battery-JV exit
Issued EUR4.9bn-equivalent of hybrid perpetual notes (three tranches, coupons 6.25%-8.25%) to shore up liquidity following the dividend suspension and negative free cash flow

Presented the FaSTLAne 2030 five-year strategic plan at Investor Day: targets EUR190bn revenue and 7% AOI margin by 2030, positive industrial FCF from 2027, and ~EUR6bn of run-rate cost cuts by 2028; four global brands (Jeep, Ram, Peugeot, FIAT) to get ~70% of product investment; plans a Dongfeng-led European JV and continued Leapmotor International and Tata partnerships

Q2/H1 2026 results showed a return to profitability (H1 net profit EUR670m vs. a EUR2.26bn net loss in H1 2025; AOI EUR1.73bn vs. EUR540m) but cash flow and cost progress disappointed investors, pressuring the stock; CEO Filosa acknowledged the turnaround will take longer than hoped

Q3 2026 trading update: estimated consolidated shipments of ~1.3 million units, down 1% YoY (Enlarged Europe +10% on BEV/Leapmotor strength; North America -12% on planned downtime ahead of the all-new 2026 Jeep Cherokee launch; Middle East & Africa -21% largely on Turkiye); FY2026 net U.S. tariff headwind estimate trimmed to EUR1.0-1.2bn (from EUR1.6bn) aided by an IEEPA tariff-refund benefit

Announced $13 billion, four-year U.S. manufacturing investment program -- the largest in company history -- including reopening the Belvidere, Illinois plant and five new vehicle launches, alongside a reiterated H2 2025 guidance of sequential improvement in revenue, AOI margin and industrial free cash flow

items.notes: Reflects expanded product portfolio and expected volume recovery; FY2025 base was EUR153.5bn
Recovering from FY2025 AOI margin of -0.5%; H1 2026 AOI margin was ~2.1% (EUR1.73bn / EUR81.6bn)
FY2025 IFCF was -EUR4.5bn; H1 2026 IFCF was -EUR0.9bn (improved from -EUR3.0bn in H1 2025); H2 2026 includes ~EUR2bn of cash payments tied to H2 2025 charges
Down from an earlier EUR1.6bn estimate, aided by an IEEPA refund benefit of ~EUR0.4bn; H1 2026 net tariff cost was EUR0.3bn
Consistent with the FaSTLAne 2030 investment plan for the year

items.target: EUR175 billion by 2028; EUR190 billion by 2030
items.notes: FaSTLAne 2030 plan baseline is FY2025 revenue of EUR154bn
Management says improvement is expected 'in the near term'

items.target: Positive by 2027; EUR3 billion by 2028; EUR6 billion by 2030

items.notes: Value Creation Program; further improvements targeted through 2030

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Antonio Filosa has repeatedly stressed that the turnaround is a multi-year process: Q3 2025 results showed the first YoY shipment/revenue growth in seven quarters and were framed as 'early signs of commercial progress,' while the Q2 2026 report (July 2026) disappointed on cash flow and cost execution, with Filosa acknowledging progress has been 'gradual' and the turnaround 'will take time.' Management has emphasized a demand-led, powertrain-flexible approach to electrification (de-emphasizing the prior 100%-EV-by-2030 European target), regional empowerment of business units, and disciplined capital allocation toward the four highest-return global brands under FaSTLAne 2030.

bull_case: New CEO Antonio Filosa's FaSTLAne 2030 plan sets a credible, conservative reset after 2025's 'kitchen sink' write-offs, with H1 2026 already showing a swing back to net profit (EUR670m vs. a EUR2.26bn loss in H1 2025) and improving AOI

$13 billion U.S. investment program and the return of higher-margin ICE/HEMI powertrains directly address the 2024-2025 product-gap and tariff-exposure problems in the company's most profitable market

Large recurring cost-reduction program (~EUR6bn run-rate by 2028) and platform/powertrain consolidation (three global platforms for ~50% of volume by 2030) offer a clear, quantified margin-recovery pathway

Valuation already reflects deep pessimism (consensus analyst ratings cluster around Hold with price targets well below 2023-2024 levels), so modest execution improvement could re-rate the stock from a low base

Diversified brand and geographic portfolio (NAFTA, Europe, South America, MEA) gives management levers to reallocate capital toward the regions (South America, Middle East & Africa) that are already delivering double-digit AOI margins
bear_case: Three straight years of market-share losses in the two most important profit pools (U.S. and EU30) show the turnaround has not yet stopped the bleeding, and FaSTLAne 2030's 2028-2030 targets depend on execution the company has repeatedly missed since the 2021 merger

Negative industrial free cash flow masked only by EUR4.9bn of new hybrid perpetual notes (6.25%-8.25% coupons) issued in Q1 2026 -- without that issuance the net cash position would have shrunk, not grown -- and the expensive coupons plus credit rating cuts (S&P BBB-, Moody's Baa3) signal real underlying balance-sheet strain
Dividend suspension removes a key support for income-oriented holders and signals management's own low confidence in near-term cash generation
U.S. tariffs on Mexico/Canada-built vehicles (including the new Jeep Cherokee) remain a structural, policy-dependent cost headwind of roughly EUR1-1.2bn annually with limited company control

Minimal China/Asia Pacific scale (<0.3% share) leaves Stellantis dependent on partners in the world's largest and fastest-moving EV market, a disadvantage versus Western peers with larger JV footprints and against Chinese entrants expanding into Europe
